headline: Coldframe honeypot mimics supermarket fridge controller to trap hackers
summary: New Python tool emulates vulnerable refrigeration supervisors, logging attacker attempts and exploits without revealing real systems.
details: Coldframe is a new honeypot designed to mimic internet-facing refrigeration supervisors, specifically targeting vulnerabilities exploited in 2026 to force defrost cycles. It poses as a supermarket fridge controller, meticulously recording any connection attempts, password guesses, and public exploits used by attackers.

The tool features two personas: Danfoss and Dixell. The Danfoss persona replicates real AK-SM 800A units, including their server headers, page titles, and TLS configurations. It even simulates weak login credentials and a specific CVE-2025-41450 exploit, providing attackers with a fake dashboard.

The Dixell persona emulates XWEB EVO units, mimicking their login flow and security headers. It also logs attempts at the XWEB Pro auth_mode bypass (CVE-2026-25085), ensuring that any malicious activity is captured and analyzed.

Coldframe is built as a single Python file with no external dependencies, making it easy to deploy. It can optionally run a Modbus TCP service to simulate fake case temperatures and setpoints, further enhancing its ability to attract and log generic industrial scanners.

The honeypot logs all attacker actions, including exploit attempts, as control events. It can be deployed on a cloud server and configured to mimic specific vendor fingerprints, providing valuable insights into the tactics used by threat actors targeting industrial control systems.

headline: iPhone Security settings to change for better data protection
summary: Learn how to enhance your iPhone's security with simple adjustments to protect your personal data from unauthorized access.
details: Your iPhone's Lock Screen can expose sensitive information like Control Center and Siri access even when locked. By default, anyone can use these features, potentially leading to pranks or making a lost device harder to find. Adjusting notification previews to show only when unlocked and disabling access to Control Center and Siri from the Lock Screen significantly enhances privacy.

Many apps request broad permissions upon first use, often leading users to grant access to location, camera, or photos without careful consideration. iOS's Safety Check feature, found in Privacy & Security settings, allows you to review and manage app permissions. You can revoke access for apps that don't require it, ensuring your sensitive information is better protected.

For deeper privacy control, navigate to Privacy & Security settings to examine individual app permissions. Setting location access to 'While Using' instead of 'Always' and disabling 'Precise Location' can prevent apps from tracking your exact whereabouts unless necessary. The App Privacy Report provides insights into how often apps access your location, microphone, or other data.

To prevent unauthorized access to specific apps, iOS allows you to lock them with Face ID or Touch ID. This is particularly useful for payment apps or sensitive information apps, protecting against scenarios where someone might borrow your unlocked phone. Apps requiring authentication will prompt for Face ID or Touch ID every time they are opened.

iOS also offers the ability to hide apps from your Home Screen, moving them to a hidden folder within the App Library that requires authentication to access. This feature is useful for apps you prefer to keep private. Remember that while these features enhance security, they should be used in conjunction with strong passcodes and up-to-date iOS versions.
